I'm approving T415 (91d2f6c0 against fe1508d3). It meets every acceptance item and changes no engine or web code. I didn't run any tests myself because this review session is read-only. The runner's own check passed: typecheck, lint, format:check and `vitest --changed` (98 files, 810 tests), all under the default config. The worker reports that worlds.test.ts also passes (4 tests) under the release-on config; the runner didn't run that, and I checked it by reading the code instead.

The risk reason was the autopilot decision of 2026-10-24 that is still waiting for the owner: every test names its release, and a release-on vitest config checks each file with the switch both on and off. The change follows that decision exactly, adds no new planning decisions, and only touches test setup, so it doesn't lock out the alternatives.

What I checked in the code:
- `DISABLED_RELEASE` and `ENABLED_RELEASE` are copies of the release object, so they keep their own on/off value whatever the switch is.
- `simulatedWorld(input, span, release = MATCH_MODEL_RELEASE)` puts the release in its cache ID and passes it through every nested build. The engine only reads the release in `createWorld` and the host constructor, and season rollover never reads it, so a world built with a given release stays on that release.
- `cached` reads `MATCH_MODEL_RELEASE.enabled` when it runs and adds it to the key for both the memory and the disk cache.
- The engine's release object isn't frozen, and the setup file and the tests import the same object.
- `vitest.release-on.config.ts` merges the base config, which has no setupFiles, workspaces or projects. The tsconfig includes root `*.ts` files and allows `.ts` imports. The `package.json` script matches the acceptance text exactly.
- The cache-separation test flips the switch inside one case and restores it in `finally`. That is safe because cases in a file run one after another and the base config keeps each file in its own worker. The task notes say only the setup file should change the switch; this test-only flip goes beyond that, but the worker disclosed it, it is scoped to one case, and it proves the separation within a single run.

There are two optional suggestions and nothing that needs fixing.

Those worlds don't depend on the global switch, so the switch-off and release-on runs can't share them. That includes the `DISABLED_RELEASE` worlds that T417 will use for most shared engine worlds. Running both test tiers therefore builds and stores each of these worlds twice, which matters given the known problem of the world cache filling the disk. This follows the acceptance as written and doesn't affect T420's cold-vs-cold gate. Optional, for T420 to weigh against its warm timings: hash the effective release instead, i.e. the explicit one for `simulatedWorld` and the default for `cachedWorld`.

If the release were dropped from the nested `simulatedWorld(…, release)` calls for seasons or rounds, the default would quietly take over, and none of the tests would catch it under either config. (2) The new browser helper starts recording after the clock has resumed, while the seek often lands only milliseconds of 1x play before the dead ball, so the new stable-controls journey is likely to fail in the batch run. findings.message: The fallback kick is 'the last phase:restart sample more than 0.1 s before the landing'. But the engine also gives the delivery flight phase 'restart': legsOf returns `phase: restart ? 'restart' : …` for spot entries, and knotted's flights use that leg phase. Every candidate minute also keeps a sample at its own end (instants keeps `to` = start+60). On the candidate the taker is never a holder before the kick (the kick knot adds a `rest`, not a `hold`), so the fallback is the main path there. Whenever a minute boundary falls between the kick and the landing, the minute-end sample becomes `to`. The kick→boundary part of the delivery (and the T359 kick sample) is then drawn at D/1500. At 1x a 25–30 s preparation makes that part 3–4× faster; at 2x, 1.7–2×. This breaks WEB-32 and the task goal ('nothing else on the timeline changed'). With deliveries of 0.15–5.6 s and about 70 prepared restarts per candidate match, this should happen about once or twice a match. Fix: count only restart samples where the ball is still on its spot (e.g. sample `ball` within a small tolerance of the restart event's `from`, which is its mirrored spot), or read the kick from the ball track. Add a unit case where a candidate corner's delivery crosses a minute end (restart sample at 60 with the ball off the spot) and assert that `to` is the kick sample.

findings.message: The helper seeks to the last sample at or before `from`, clicks 1× (which resumes playback), and only then starts the rAF recorder in a separate `canvas.evaluate`. On the pre-feature path there is always a sample at the ball going dead (P.times are kept), and the event's t is that time rounded to a tenth. About half the time that sample lies 0–0.05 s before `from`, which is under 10 ms at 1x. The first recorded `data-seconds` is then already past `from`, `enteredAt` is -1, and 'the clock reached the dead ball' fails. Even otherwise the margin is the gap to the previous sample (≈1 s of match time, about 200 ms at 1x), close to a click plus a CDP round trip. Seeds are fixed, so the new stable-pace journey would fail every time in the pre-push batch rather than flake. Seek to a sample a few match seconds before `from` (e.g. `times.findLastIndex(t => t <= from - 3)`), or start the recorder before clicking 1× and collect afterwards. Run the journey once on chromium before handing it to the batch.

kindOf checks the outcome before the spot. A restart entry whose delivery is flagged offside, or ends in a foul, is recorded as kind 'offside'/'foul' while still carrying `restart: 'freeKick'` (playback.ts sets ev.restart for any spot entry). Its actor is then the receiver or the fouler, not the taker. The `kind === 'restart'` filter skips these free kicks, so their preparation keeps running speed even though WEB-32 covers every free kick. The acceptance itself names `kind: 'restart'`, so this is a planning gap: either key on `event.restart` and resolve the taker another way, or record the exception in the task or SSOT.

The comment 'Every minute takes exactly 12 s at 1x, whatever happens in it' stopped being true once T422 added preparations. At 2x, a corner, free kick or goal kick preparation of 39 s or more inside the first minute would end '1′' before the 3.6 s check. That is rare but possible if the founding seed varies. Reword the comment, and either pick the first minute knowing it has no long preparation or derive the bound with presentationMs and the playback's preparations.

The recording slack is the literal `+ 1500`, the same value as SET_PIECE_PREPARATION_MS, which the impl note wants to stay the only preparation number. It reads as the preparation time. Name it as slack (or derive it from SET_PIECE_PREPARATION_MS) so the owner's later tuning cannot leave a stale twin.

Two autopilot decisions are waiting for the owner, as the risk flags note. (a) The kick is read from the taker's take or the last restart sample, not the restart event's t (the impl note's literal 'kick = the restart event's own time' would compress the delivery). (b) Measured match lengths are 14.3–15.9 min at 1x and 8.0–8.6 min at 2x, against WEB-32's 'about 13–14 / 7'. Neither blocks the code. Hand both to the owner's in-play review of SET_PIECE_PREPARATION_MS (ideation/match-viewing-pace-and-freedom) instead of changing the number here.

Its from and the resolution use the kick spot. commentary.ts:72 names cellName(entry.cell), so after a carry that crosses a cell edge (mean carry 3.94 m) a pass is narrated from the wrong cell. Shots, crosses and cut-backs are kept in their cell, so mostly passes are affected. Optional fix: trace the tags play() recomputes at the kick spot, or recompute them after the carry.

After a carry the kick happens at once (windUp 0, kick at start, engine.ts:484), so any slack between the leftover action time and the actual flight lengthens the flight. That slack comes from the 0.2 s step floor, the carry shortening the pass, or the receiver's reach (for example through balls and interceptions), and the ball then travels below its GRID_BALL_CONFIG speed. This breaks no rule, since speeds are only capped from above. Worth measuring the drawn ball-speed distribution when T437 or T435 tunes the candidate.

findings.message: Hand-off for the planner and T437, not a fix. Under the worker's reading of the build-up shares, the reacher gets a failed pass only on the tactic's draw (0.155–0.195 below 70 m), however much time he has to spare. A full-weight reacher costs the pass only LANE_CONFIG.risk (0.033) of completion. So a defender standing squarely in the lane lets most passes through him: reached passes still complete at 78.7%. The round-69 result shows 77% of failed passes are reached, yet only 10.1% end in the lane; the rest fly past the reacher and are lost at the receiver. MATCH-31's rationale calls 'one standing in the lane who lets it through' no defending. The acceptance fixes this structure (completion held at its frame, shares kept), and the worker recorded the reading and the levers (intercept shares, sure, stretch, weight). When T437 recalibrates, the planner should confirm whether the shares should be rescaled to the reached failures or the cut-out tied to spare.

On a pass with no in-stride carry (keeper distributions and first-time balls, 3.1% of passes), the reach is computed with kickAt = least − the flight to the pass's end. motionOf's windUp is dt − the flight to where the ball actually ended. For an interception or deflection that flight is shorter, so playback kicks later and the ball reaches the reach point later than reachOnPath assumed, by the uncovered part of the flight. The other defenders' playback read (readAt on windUp) uses the same later kick. This never shows a reach that could not happen; it only gives the interceptor more time than the engine credited him. Note it for T442/T437, which reuse reachOnPath's timing: either time the reach from the same wind-up motionOf will use, or record why the gap is acceptable.

passOptions' reach risk also drives the target choice for crosses and cut-backs, because choosePass runs with { crossOnly: true } at decide.ts:888. The result lists only choosePass for passes, keeper distribution and restarts. A cross is lofted, but its target choice now weighs a ground-speed reach of its path, as the old exp(−d/2) term did. The round-69 figures already include this, so it is not a regression. Note it for T444, which rewrites delivery choice and reads reachOnPath for deliveries, so that its 'before' is measured with this in place.

The pre-feature path and its digests are unchanged, and the runner's checks passed (typecheck, lint, format:check, vitest --changed: 219 files, 1704 tests). findings.message: On the candidate model, `marker` is dropped for every pass, and `markerSkill` becomes the first reacher's 위치선정, or 60 when nobody reaches the path. resolvePass also handles keeper distributions: decide.ts:877 sends a keeper's open-play pass through play(), and restarts.ts:324 sends goal kicks (`keeper` = GK). MATCH-11 r28 changed only the short/long/switch pass row to 'the opponent who reaches its path first'. The keeper distribution row still says 'the defender nearest the lane'. With P.marker at 1/300, the nearest defender's 위치선정 moves a keeper pass's completion by up to about ±10 points, and a keeper ball with no reacher now ignores him entirely. Fix: on the candidate, when `keeper` is true, keep `nearestToSegment(...)`'s 위치선정 as the marker. Leave the lane term and the cut-out on `reachOnPath`. Add a resolve test that a keeper's completion follows the defender nearest the lane even when nobody reaches the path, then re-record the candidate digests. If planning wants keeper distributions on the reach rule too, MATCH-11's keeper row must change first; this is for the planner to decide, not the worker.

'nobody cuts out a pass he could not reach' cannot fail under the old rule; the worker's limit (5) says so. motionOf lengthens the action until the new owner reaches the ball, so the next play always starts at the reach point. The carry-only check uses the fastest anyone runs, with no acceleration or read. A stronger version would rebuild each interception from its kick-time places and check that the interceptor gets within `stretch` of `at` by the ball's pass-speed arrival. That would let the fixture test catch an interception by someone who could not have got there.

`diagnostics.passLosses` and the `PassLosses` export are written but nothing in the repo reads them; the round-69 shares came from scratch probes. Either pin them with a test (in one fixture, the four counts add up to that side's failed open-play passes) or have the calibration scripts report them, so T437 can use them. Otherwise remove them. `laneWeight` and `runSeconds` are also exported with no reader outside lanes.ts.

On both models that time is actually when the delivery lands, so following it would also speed up the delivery, which WEB-32 and MATCH-12 keep at the selected speed. Instead the kick is read from data both models carry:
- pre-feature: the moment the taker takes the ball, from `holders`

findings.message: The fallback kick is 'the last phase:restart sample more than 0.1 s before the landing'. But the engine also gives the delivery flight phase 'restart': legsOf returns `phase: restart ? 'restart' : …` for spot entries, and knotted's flights use that leg phase. Every candidate minute also keeps a sample at its own end (instants keeps `to` = start+60). On the candidate the taker is never a holder before the kick (the kick knot adds a `rest`, not a `hold`), so the fallback is the main path there. Whenever a minute boundary falls between the kick and the landing, the minute-end sample becomes `to`. The kick→boundary part of the delivery (and the T359 kick sample) is then drawn at D/1500. At 1x a 25–30 s preparation makes that part 3–4× faster; at 2x, 1.7–2×. This breaks WEB-32 and the task goal ('nothing else on the timeline changed'). With deliveries of 0.15–5.6 s and about 70 prepared restarts per candidate match, this should happen about once or twice a match. Fix: count only restart samples where the ball is still on its spot (e.g. sample `ball` within a small tolerance of the restart event's `from`, which is its mirrored spot), or read the kick from the ball track. Add a unit case where a candidate corner's delivery crosses a minute end (restart sample at 60 with the ball off the spot) and assert that `to` is the kick sample.

findings.message: The helper seeks to the last sample at or before `from`, clicks 1× (which resumes playback), and only then starts the rAF recorder in a separate `canvas.evaluate`. On the pre-feature path there is always a sample at the ball going dead (P.times are kept), and the event's t is that time rounded to a tenth. About half the time that sample lies 0–0.05 s before `from`, which is under 10 ms at 1x. The first recorded `data-seconds` is then already past `from`, `enteredAt` is -1, and 'the clock reached the dead ball' fails. Even otherwise the margin is the gap to the previous sample (≈1 s of match time, about 200 ms at 1x), close to a click plus a CDP round trip. Seeds are fixed, so the new stable-pace journey would fail every time in the pre-push batch rather than flake. Seek to a sample a few match seconds before `from` (e.g. `times.findLastIndex(t => t <= from - 3)`), or start the recorder before clicking 1× and collect afterwards. Run the journey once on chromium before handing it to the batch.

kindOf checks the outcome before the spot. A restart entry whose delivery is flagged offside, or ends in a foul, is recorded as kind 'offside'/'foul' while still carrying `restart: 'freeKick'` (playback.ts sets ev.restart for any spot entry). Its actor is then the receiver or the fouler, not the taker. The `kind === 'restart'` filter skips these free kicks, so their preparation keeps running speed even though WEB-32 covers every free kick. The acceptance itself names `kind: 'restart'`, so this is a planning gap: either key on `event.restart` and resolve the taker another way, or record the exception in the task or SSOT.

The comment 'Every minute takes exactly 12 s at 1x, whatever happens in it' stopped being true once T422 added preparations. At 2x, a corner, free kick or goal kick preparation of 39 s or more inside the first minute would end '1′' before the 3.6 s check. That is rare but possible if the founding seed varies. Reword the comment, and either pick the first minute knowing it has no long preparation or derive the bound with presentationMs and the playback's preparations.

The recording slack is the literal `+ 1500`, the same value as SET_PIECE_PREPARATION_MS, which the impl note wants to stay the only preparation number. It reads as the preparation time. Name it as slack (or derive it from SET_PIECE_PREPARATION_MS) so the owner's later tuning cannot leave a stale twin.

Two autopilot decisions are waiting for the owner, as the risk flags note. (a) The kick is read from the taker's take or the last restart sample, not the restart event's t (the impl note's literal 'kick = the restart event's own time' would compress the delivery). (b) Measured match lengths are 14.3–15.9 min at 1x and 8.0–8.6 min at 2x, against WEB-32's 'about 13–14 / 7'. Neither blocks the code. Hand both to the owner's in-play review of SET_PIECE_PREPARATION_MS (ideation/match-viewing-pace-and-freedom) instead of changing the number here.

It returns the opponent the ball meets first, his spare time (the most time in hand from that point on) and the summed weights of everyone who reaches the path.

|---|---|---|

The carry-only check uses the fastest anyone runs, with no acceleration or read. A stronger version would rebuild each interception from its kick-time places and check that the interceptor gets within `stretch` of `at` by the ball's pass-speed arrival. That would let the fixture test catch an interception by someone who could not have got there.

findings.message: Hand-off for the planner and T437, not a fix. Under the worker's reading of the build-up shares, the reacher gets a failed pass only on the tactic's draw (0.155–0.195 below 70 m), however much time he has to spare. A full-weight reacher costs the pass only LANE_CONFIG.risk (0.033) of completion. So a defender standing squarely in the lane lets most passes through him: reached passes still complete at 78.7%. The round-69 result shows 77% of failed passes are reached, yet only 10.1% end in the lane; the rest fly past the reacher and are lost at the receiver. MATCH-31's rationale calls 'one standing in the lane who lets it through' no defending. The acceptance fixes this structure (completion held at its frame, shares kept), and the worker recorded the reading and the levers (intercept shares, sure, stretch, weight). When T437 recalibrates, the planner should confirm whether the shares should be rescaled to the reached failures or the cut-out tied to spare.

On a pass with no in-stride carry (keeper distributions and first-time balls, 3.1% of passes), the reach is computed with kickAt = least − the flight to the pass's end. motionOf's windUp is dt − the flight to where the ball actually ended. For an interception or deflection that flight is shorter, so playback kicks later and the ball reaches the reach point later than reachOnPath assumed, by the uncovered part of the flight. The other defenders' playback read (readAt on windUp) uses the same later kick. This never shows a reach that could not happen; it only gives the interceptor more time than the engine credited him. Note it for T442/T437, which reuse reachOnPath's timing: either time the reach from the same wind-up motionOf will use, or record why the gap is acceptable.

passOptions' reach risk also drives the target choice for crosses and cut-backs, because choosePass runs with { crossOnly: true } at decide.ts:888. The result lists only choosePass for passes, keeper distribution and restarts. A cross is lofted, but its target choice now weighs a ground-speed reach of its path, as the old exp(−d/2) term did. The round-69 figures already include this, so it is not a regression. Note it for T444, which rewrites delivery choice and reads reachOnPath for deliveries, so that its 'before' is measured with this in place.
